questions.question: A startup uses the AWS root user for daily deployments. A security audit flags this as critical. What is the PRIMARY reason this is dangerous?

options.text: Root user credentials cannot be used with the AWS CLI
The root user is unconstrained by any IAM policy, SCP, or permission boundary — a compromised credential gives full account control with no recovery path
Root user actions are not logged in CloudTrail
Root user access keys expire after 90 days

explanation.correct: The root user bypasses every IAM control. If compromised, the attacker can reverse every defensive measure. No recovery short of account closure.
explanation.why: Root actions ARE logged. CLI works with root. Keys don't auto-expire. The danger is the absolute lack of policy constraints.

questions.question: An IAM role trust policy says Principal: AWS: arn:aws:iam::222222222222:root, Action: sts:AssumeRole. An EC2 instance in account 222 with instance profile AppRole tries to assume this role. What happens?

options.text: Success — the trust policy allows the entire account so all principals in it may assume the role automatically
Success only if AppRole has an identity-based policy explicitly allowing sts:AssumeRole on this role ARN
Failure — only the literal root user can assume roles via :root trust policies
Failure — instance profiles cannot call sts:AssumeRole

explanation.correct: Granting :root means any principal in that account CAN be delegated assume permission — but the calling principal must also have an explicit Allow for sts:AssumeRole on this role ARN. Both sides required.
explanation.why: Option A is the classic misread. :root does not auto-allow everyone — it allows the account to delegate assumption rights to its principals.

questions.question: Role R has: identity-based policy allowing s3:GetObject, permission boundary allowing s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject, bucket policy with no statement for role R (same account). What is R's effective permission for s3:GetObject?

options.text: Denied — the bucket policy must also explicitly allow role R for same-account access
Allowed — identity-based Allow intersects with boundary (both allow it), bucket policy has no Deny, same-account rule applies
Denied — permission boundaries must contain matching statements to bucket policies
Allowed — the permission boundary alone grants access independent of identity-based policy

explanation.correct: Effective permissions = intersection of identity-based AND boundary. Both allow GetObject. Bucket policy has no Deny. Same-account: resource-based Allow not required if identity-based side is covered.
explanation.why: Permission boundaries do not need to match bucket policies. Absence of a bucket policy statement is fine for same-account.

questions.question: A security engineer is writing an S3 bucket policy to grant access to a set of developers. She tries to set the Principal to the IAM group DevTeamGroup. The policy fails to save with a validation error. What is the correct explanation and fix?

options.text: IAM groups are not identities — they cannot be Principals in resource-based policies. She must reference the individual IAM users or the IAM role that developers assume instead.
Group ARNs must be prefixed with group/ in the Principal — change to arn:aws:iam::123456789012:group/DevTeamGroup and the policy will work.
S3 bucket policies do not support IAM principals from the same account — she must use an IAM role from a different account.
The group must first be attached to the bucket as an ACL grantee before it can be used as a bucket policy Principal.

explanation.correct: IAM groups are permission management containers — not identities. They have no ARN that can be used as a Principal in any resource-based policy. The correct fix is to reference the IAM role that developers assume or their individual user ARNs.
explanation.why: B is wrong — there is no valid 'group/' ARN format for bucket policy Principals. C is wrong — same-account IAM principals are fully supported. D is wrong — ACLs are a separate, legacy mechanism.

questions.question: A solutions architect is designing a Lambda function that reads raw data from an S3 bucket, writes transformed results to a DynamoDB table, and publishes completion events to an SNS topic. A security reviewer says the execution role should have its Resource elements scoped to exact ARNs and should contain only three IAM actions. The architect argues that using s3:*, dynamodb:*, and sns:* with specific resource ARNs is simpler and still least-privilege on the resource axis. Who is correct?

options.text: The architect — scoping the Resource to specific ARNs is the only dimension that matters for least privilege; the Action scope does not need to be minimized.

The security reviewer — least privilege requires both narrow Action scope AND narrow Resource scope. s3:* includes DeleteBucket and PutBucketPolicy which the function never needs; both axes must be minimized.
Both are correct — the SAA-C03 exam accepts either approach as equivalent least privilege.
The architect — AWS managed policies like AmazonS3FullAccess are designed for Lambda and implicitly apply resource-level restrictions.

explanation.correct: Least privilege requires minimizing BOTH the action scope AND the resource scope independently. s3:* grants dangerous admin-level S3 actions (DeleteBucket, PutBucketPolicy, PutBucketAcl) the function never calls. The correct execution role has exactly s3:GetObject, dynamodb:PutItem, and sns:Publish on their specific ARNs.
explanation.why: A fails because wide action scope on a narrow resource still allows destructive actions on that resource. AWS managed policies (D) grant far too many permissions for workload roles. The two-axis grading rubric applies to both axes independently.

questions.question: A bucket policy explicitly allows s3:GetObject for DevRole in the same account. DevRole has no identity-based S3 policy. Can DevRole call GetObject?

options.text: No — identity-based policy must also explicitly allow s3:GetObject for same-account access
Yes — for same-account access, a resource-based Allow in the bucket policy is sufficient without an identity-based Allow
No — bucket policies can only grant access to external accounts, not same-account roles
Yes — but only if DevRole has no permission boundary attached

explanation.correct: Same-account rule: if the bucket policy explicitly allows the role, access is granted even without an identity-based Allow. One explicit Allow (either side) is sufficient for same-account. Cross-account requires both sides.
explanation.why: Option A describes the cross-account requirement, not same-account. Bucket policies can grant same-account role access.

questions.question: A compliance policy states audit logs must be immutable for 7 years and no user including administrators may delete them. Which mechanism enforces this MOST completely?

options.text: IAM policy with explicit Deny on s3:DeleteObject attached to all admin roles
S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode plus a bucket policy explicit Deny on s3:DeleteObject and s3:PutLifecycleConfiguration
Permission boundaries on all IAM users restricting s3:DeleteObject
SCP denying s3:DeleteObject for all accounts in the organization

explanation.correct: S3 Object Lock Compliance mode makes objects truly immutable — even root cannot delete them within retention. The bucket policy Deny adds an IAM-layer guard.
explanation.why: A, C, D all rely on IAM controls a sufficiently privileged principal could remove. Object Lock Compliance is enforced at the S3 service level and cannot be overridden by any IAM policy.

questions.question: A developer policy has: Effect: Allow, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::reports. They call GetObject on reports/Q4.csv and get Access Denied. Why?

options.text: The developer does not have MFA enabled
s3:GetObject is an object-level action requiring an object ARN like reports/*, not the bucket-level ARN (reports) which covers no objects
Cross-region access is blocked by default
The bucket policy overrides the identity-based policy

explanation.correct: s3:GetObject needs arn:aws:s3:::reports/* or arn:aws:s3:::reports/Q4.csv. The bucket ARN arn:aws:s3:::reports (no trailing path) only matches bucket-level actions like s3:ListBucket. Action-to-ARN type mismatch.
explanation.why: One of the most common S3 policy mistakes. MFA, cross-region, and bucket policy overrides are not the issue here.

questions.question: A bucket policy has: Effect: Deny, Principal: *, Action: s3:DeleteObject, NotResource: arn:aws:s3:::prod-backups/retained/*. What does this accomplish?

options.text: Denies s3:DeleteObject on EVERYTHING EXCEPT prod-backups/retained/ — deletion is blocked on all other objects
Denies s3:DeleteObject only on objects in the prod-backups/retained/ prefix
Allows s3:DeleteObject on prod-backups/retained/ while denying all other delete operations on that same prefix only
The NotResource element is invalid syntax in Deny statements

explanation.correct: NotResource inverts the resource match. Effect: Deny + NotResource: prod-backups/retained/* = Deny DeleteObject on everything NOT in that prefix. Objects in retained/ are excluded from the Deny.
explanation.why: NotResource is valid in both Allow and Deny. It inverts which resources the statement applies to.

questions.question: Account 111 has a KMS key. Account 222 needs to decrypt data encrypted with it. Architect configures: (1) KMS key policy in Account 111 allows Account 222. (2) IAM role in Account 222 allows kms:Decrypt on the key ARN. Is this sufficient without role assumption via STS?

options.text: No — STS cross-account role assumption is also required before kms:Decrypt can be called
Yes — KMS key policy (destination) plus IAM role policy (source) satisfy the two-pronged requirement; no STS assumption needed for direct cross-account KMS usage
No — the KMS key must be replicated to Account 222 first
No — an SCP in Account 222 must also explicitly allow kms:Decrypt

explanation.correct: Direct cross-account KMS: key policy in key's account must allow external principal, AND the IAM identity in calling account must have kms:Decrypt. Both together are sufficient without STS role assumption.
explanation.why: Cross-account KMS access can work directly without role assumption. STS is needed for role assumption patterns, not direct cross-account KMS usage.

questions.question: A company wants developers who write their own application role policies to never be able to grant more than read access to production S3, even if a developer writes s3:*. Which mechanism enforces this ceiling automatically?

options.text: A production bucket policy with explicit Deny on write operations for all developer roles
A permission boundary on developer-managed roles permitting only s3:Get* and s3:List* on production buckets
An SCP on the developer OU denying s3:Put* and s3:Delete*
Both B and C are valid; B applies per-role while C applies per-account

explanation.correct: Permission boundaries (B) cap the maximum permissions of specific IAM roles. SCPs (C) apply to all principals in the account/OU. Both work; the difference is per-role vs per-account scope.
explanation.why: A bucket policy Deny could be removed by anyone with s3:PutBucketPolicy. Permission boundaries and SCPs are harder to circumvent and apply automatically.

questions.question: Which statement CORRECTLY describes aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent vs aws:MultiFactorAuthAge?

options.text: MultiFactorAuthPresent checks if MFA is registered; MultiFactorAuthAge checks if it was used at login

MultiFactorAuthPresent is a Boolean set to true at session start when MFA was used, stays true all session; MultiFactorAuthAge is numeric seconds elapsed since MFA was issued and increases throughout the session
MultiFactorAuthAge is Boolean; MultiFactorAuthPresent is numeric seconds — they are reversed
Both are interchangeable aliases for the same condition

explanation.correct: Present: Boolean, set at session start, stays true the entire session. Age: numeric seconds since MFA issued, increases as session ages. Use NumericLessThan: 900 with Age to require fresh MFA within 15 minutes.
explanation.why: They are completely different types with different security properties. Present does not protect against session hijacking. Age does.

questions.question: A company enforces MFA at sign-in and adds aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true to all deletion policies. A pen tester says this is insufficient against session hijacking. Why is the tester correct?

options.text: MultiFactorAuthPresent: true only works for S3 deletion, not other services
A stolen session token from a user who authenticated with MFA 8 hours ago still has MultiFactorAuthPresent: true — the check passes for the entire session lifetime regardless of session age
The condition key name should be aws:MultiFactorAuthenticated, not MultiFactorAuthPresent
MFA conditions cannot be applied to deletion policies

explanation.correct: MultiFactorAuthPresent is set at session start and never changes. A hijacked 8-hour-old session token still passes the Present check. aws:MultiFactorAuthAge with a small threshold (e.g. 300) forces re-authentication recency.
explanation.why: Present offers no recency guarantee. Age is the correct control for high-risk operations.

questions.question: A policy has: Effect: Allow, Action: s3:*, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*. A developer calls s3:ListBucket on my-bucket and the call fails. Why?

options.text: s3:* only covers object-level permissions; ListBucket is not included in the wildcard
s3:ListBucket requires MFA by default
s3:ListBucket is a bucket-level operation requiring the bucket ARN (arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket), not the object ARN (my-bucket/*). The policy resource only covers objects.
s3:ListBucket is not included in s3:*

explanation.correct: s3:ListBucket needs arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket (no trailing path). The policy resource arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/* covers only object operations. For both, include both ARNs: bucket ARN and bucket/* ARN.
explanation.why: s3:* does include ListBucket. The failure is purely the ARN type mismatch.

questions.question: A security team manually audits IAM policies monthly and finds unintended S3 bucket access after a cross-account role assumption was granted three weeks ago. They want continuous, automated detection of unintended resource exposure without requiring policy review cycles. Which AWS service specifically addresses this?

options.text: AWS Config with the s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited rule — continuously evaluates bucket ACLs and bucket policies for public access.

IAM Access Analyzer — uses automated formal reasoning to continuously identify resources reachable from outside the zone of trust, including cross-account and public access paths through bucket policies, KMS key policies, and role trust policies.
Amazon GuardDuty — detects when S3 objects are accessed by unusual principals and generates threat intelligence findings.
AWS Security Hub — aggregates findings from multiple security services and applies compliance frameworks to identify gaps.

explanation.correct: IAM Access Analyzer uses automated formal reasoning to continuously model who can access which resources — including through bucket policies, trust policies, and KMS key policies — and generates findings whenever access from outside the zone of trust is possible, even before it is actually exercised.
explanation.why: Config (A) checks specific rules like public ACLs but doesn't reason about complex cross-account role chains. GuardDuty (C) detects runtime anomalies but requires access to actually occur. Security Hub (D) aggregates findings — it doesn't generate them. Access Analyzer is the only service that reasons about potential access paths proactively.

questions.question: Three policies apply: SCP (no S3 statement), identity-based (explicit Allow s3:GetObject on bucket A), bucket policy (explicit Deny s3:GetObject for the role). What is the result?

options.text: Allow — SCP has no statement so no restriction; identity-based Allow is effective
Deny — bucket policy explicit Deny triggers Step 1 of the evaluation rule; all Allows are irrelevant
Allow — identity-based policies take precedence over resource-based in same-account
Deny — SCP with no S3 statement is treated as implicit Deny

explanation.correct: Step 1: any explicit Deny anywhere? Yes — bucket policy explicit Deny. Evaluation stops. Denied. The identity-based Allow and SCP silence are both irrelevant.
explanation.why: SCP silence is NOT a Deny. The bucket policy explicit Deny is the sole reason for denial.

questions.question: Account A calls s3:GetObject on a bucket in Account B. The Account B bucket policy grants Account A's role access. The Account A role has no identity-based S3 policy. What is the result?

options.text: Allowed — the bucket policy in Account B is sufficient for cross-account access
Denied — cross-account requires explicit Allow on both sides; the source account role has no s3:GetObject permission
Allowed — bucket policies override identity-based policies for cross-account calls
Denied — cross-account S3 always requires STS role assumption first

explanation.correct: Cross-account requires explicit Allow on both sides. Account B bucket policy = destination side present. Account A role = source side has no Allow. Implicit deny at the source.
explanation.why: Same-account: one explicit Allow (either side) is enough. Cross-account: BOTH sides must explicitly Allow. This is the fundamental cross-account rule.

questions.question: A security team wants: even if a developer creates a new IAM role with AdministratorAccess, that role cannot access production S3 buckets. Must apply automatically to all future roles. Best approach?

options.text: Attach a permission boundary to every new IAM role that excludes production S3
Apply an SCP to the developer account OU denying s3:* on production bucket ARNs — applies automatically to every principal including new roles
Add an explicit Deny to every production bucket policy listing all developer account role ARNs
Use IAM Access Analyzer to detect and alert on new roles accessing production buckets

explanation.correct: An SCP on the developer OU applies automatically to ALL principals — including new roles with AdministratorAccess. SCP Deny cannot be overridden by any identity-based Allow. Zero per-role action required.
explanation.why: Permission boundaries (A) must be manually attached to each new role. Bucket policy Denies (C) require manual per-bucket updates. Access Analyzer (D) detects but does not prevent.

questions.question: EC2 in Account B (instance profile with sts:AssumeRole on ProdRole in Account 111) tries to read an encrypted S3 object. ProdRole has s3:GetObject on prod-bucket. The KMS key in Account 111 has NO policy entry for ProdRole. What happens?

options.text: Success — ProdRole has s3:GetObject and no bucket policy Deny is mentioned
Access Denied on kms:Decrypt — S3 GetObject succeeds but decryption fails because the KMS key policy does not authorize ProdRole for kms:Decrypt
Access Denied on AssumeRole — the trust policy must list the specific role ARN from Account B
Access Denied on GetObject — bucket policy is always required for cross-account S3 access via assumed roles

explanation.correct: AssumeRole succeeds. GetObject succeeds. S3 returns the encrypted object and SDK automatically calls kms:Decrypt. KMS key policy has no entry for ProdRole — Access Denied at decrypt. KMS two-pronged rule: both IAM role policy AND KMS key policy must allow kms:Decrypt.
explanation.why: The failure chain breaks at KMS. S3 GetObject succeeds but decryption fails — a very common production gotcha.

questions.question: Organization master SCP: Effect: Allow, Action: *, Resource: *. Developer account has no other SCPs. Developer's IAM policy explicitly Denies ec2:TerminateInstances. Can the developer terminate EC2?

options.text: Yes — the SCP Allow: * overrides any identity-based Deny
No — the identity-based Deny is still evaluated; the SCP Allow merely removes SCP-level restriction but cannot override explicit Denies in identity-based policies
Yes — SCPs always override identity-based policies
No — the SCP Allow: * is invalid syntax

explanation.correct: SCPs define maximum available permissions — they don't grant permissions. The identity-based Deny is evaluated under the three-step rule and wins. SCP Allow * means no SCP-level blocking, but explicit Deny in identity-based policy still applies.
explanation.why: The three-step evaluation rule applies after SCP filtering. SCP Allow * removes SCP restriction; the identity-based explicit Deny still triggers Step 1.

questions.question: An application accesses S3 in the same account. Architect wants both identity-based Allow AND bucket policy Allow. Developer says bucket policy is redundant. Who is right?

options.text: The architect — both are required in all scenarios
The developer — for same-account access, the identity-based Allow alone is sufficient; the bucket policy adds defense-in-depth but is not required to grant access
The architect — the bucket policy is required to complete the resource-side authorization even for same-account access to ensure the two-pronged rule is met
Both are wrong — same-account S3 access always requires both an identity-based Allow AND a bucket policy Allow regardless of account configuration

explanation.correct: Same-account: identity-based Allow alone is sufficient as long as no Deny exists. Bucket policy is not required. Adding it is defense-in-depth but not necessary.
explanation.why: The developer is correct. The 'both required' rule only applies to cross-account access.

questions.question: A company has 5 AWS accounts. Engineers need to read CloudWatch logs in all 5 with a single credential set and no long-lived access keys. Which architecture?

options.text: Create one IAM user per account with CloudWatch read access; distribute credentials
Use AWS IAM Identity Center with permission sets granting CloudWatch read, assigned to all 5 accounts — engineers log in once via corporate IdP and get temporary credentials per account
Create cross-account roles in each account; have engineers manually call sts:AssumeRole per account each session
Use AWS Organizations consolidated billing to share CloudWatch access

explanation.correct: IAM Identity Center provides centralized SSO with permission sets across all Organization accounts. Engineers authenticate once via corporate IdP and get temporary credentials. No long-lived credentials anywhere.
explanation.why: A creates long-lived credentials. C requires manual role assumption per account. Consolidated billing has nothing to do with access control.

questions.question: Bucket policy: Effect: Deny, Principal: *, Action: s3:PutObject, Condition: Bool: aws:SecureTransport: false. What does this enforce?

options.text: All PutObject calls must use HTTPS — requests over plain HTTP are denied
PutObject is denied unless the caller has MFA enabled
PutObject is denied for all cross-account principals
PutObject is denied unless the request originates from within a VPC

explanation.correct: aws:SecureTransport evaluates to true for HTTPS and false for HTTP. The policy Denies PutObject when SecureTransport is false. This forces all callers to use HTTPS for S3 uploads.
explanation.why: Standard S3 encryption-in-transit pattern. SecureTransport has nothing to do with MFA, cross-account origins, or VPC routing.

questions.question: A role trust policy has Principal: Service: lambda.amazonaws.com. A developer tries to manually assume this role from the AWS CLI. What happens?

options.text: Success — any principal who knows the role ARN can assume any role
Access Denied — the trust policy only allows the Lambda service; CLI calls use a human identity, not the Lambda service principal
Success — the AWS CLI automatically uses the lambda.amazonaws.com service namespace
Access Denied — Lambda execution roles can never be assumed by any principal

explanation.correct: The trust policy Principal is lambda.amazonaws.com. A human CLI call uses an IAM user or role identity — not the Lambda service. Trust relationship check fails.
explanation.why: Service principals (lambda.amazonaws.com) and human principals are different. Only the Lambda execution environment can assume this role.

questions.question: A policy grants iam:CreateUser, iam:AttachUserPolicy, iam:PutUserPolicy with Resource: *. Why is this a privilege escalation risk?

options.text: iam:CreateUser allows creating new users who can then be granted AdministratorAccess via iam:AttachUserPolicy — creating an admin backdoor
Resource: * makes these actions apply to all IAM resources which costs more
iam:PutUserPolicy can modify the user's own inline policy to add admin permissions directly
Both A and C are correct privilege escalation paths

explanation.correct: Two paths: (A) Create a new user and attach AdministratorAccess — you control an admin user. (C) Use iam:PutUserPolicy to modify your own inline policy to add admin permissions. Both are real IAM escalation vectors.
explanation.why: IAM permissions that allow modifying policies are extremely sensitive and should only go to dedicated admin roles with strong MFA.

questions.question: A company stores data in S3 with prefixes /finance/, /engineering/, /hr/. They want each department to access only their own prefix using a SINGLE IAM policy. What achieves this?

options.text: Create one IAM policy per prefix and attach to the corresponding group
Use IAM policy variables: Resource: arn:aws:s3:::company-bucket/${aws:PrincipalTag/Department}/* — dynamically constructed from the caller's Department tag
Create separate S3 buckets per department
Use S3 ACLs to grant prefix-level access per user

explanation.correct: IAM policy variables dynamically construct the resource ARN from principal attributes. A role tagged Department=Finance can only access /finance/* because that is what the variable resolves to. One policy, unlimited departments.
explanation.why: Per-prefix policies require manual creation and don't scale. S3 ACLs are legacy and coarse-grained.

questions.question: An auditor finds a role with: Effect: Allow, Action: NotAction: [iam:*, organizations:*], Resource: *. What does this grant?

options.text: Everything EXCEPT iam:* and organizations:* — the effective permissions are identical to PowerUserAccess but without the AWS-managed policy guardrails, meaning the developer can use all compute, storage, database, and analytics services
Only iam:* and organizations:* — NotAction with Allow means only those services
Nothing — NotAction combined with Allow is invalid IAM syntax
Everything including iam:* — NotAction on Allow equals Action: *

explanation.correct: NotAction with Effect: Allow means 'allow everything EXCEPT the listed actions.' This grants access to all AWS services and actions EXCEPT IAM and Organizations — effectively equivalent to PowerUserAccess in scope but without its managed policy update cadence. Still extremely powerful and should be flagged.
explanation.why: NotAction inverts the action match. Should be flagged as overly broad — never for regular developer roles.

questions.question: A company wants a single S3 bucket policy allowing read from any account inside their Organization without listing individual account IDs. Which condition key achieves this?

options.text: aws:SourceAccount — matches a specific source account ID
aws:PrincipalOrgID — matches any principal whose account belongs to the specified Organization ID
aws:PrincipalArn — matches ARNs with a wildcard pattern
aws:ResourceOrgID — matches resources owned by org accounts

explanation.correct: aws:PrincipalOrgID with the org ID covers all current and future member accounts automatically. New accounts that join the org are covered without any bucket policy update.
explanation.why: aws:SourceAccount matches specific account IDs. aws:PrincipalArn requires specific ARN patterns. aws:ResourceOrgID is not a standard condition key for this purpose.

questions.question: A developer role has an identity-based policy allowing s3:PutObject on logs-bucket/*. The role's permission boundary only allows s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket. Can the developer call s3:PutObject?

options.text: Yes — the identity-based policy explicitly allows PutObject
No — effective permissions = intersection of identity-based policy and permission boundary; PutObject is not in the boundary so it is excluded from effective permissions
Yes — the boundary's Resource: * overrides its action restrictions
No — permission boundaries require an explicit Deny to block actions

explanation.correct: Effective permissions = intersection. Identity-based allows PutObject. Boundary allows only GetObject and ListBucket. PutObject is NOT in the intersection. Effectively denied — not by explicit Deny but by absence from the intersection.
explanation.why: Permission boundaries do not need explicit Deny. Anything not in the boundary cannot be an effective permission.

questions.question: A Lambda needs to read from bucket A, write to bucket B, and publish to a specific SNS topic. Following least privilege, which policy is correct?

options.text: Effect: Allow, Action: lambda:*, Resource: *
Effect: Allow, Actions: s3:GetObject on bucket-A/*, s3:PutObject on bucket-B/*, sns:Publish on the specific SNS topic ARN
Effect: Allow, Action: s3:* on both buckets, sns:* on all topics
Effect: Allow, Action: s3:* on bucket-A and bucket-B, sns:Publish on all SNS topics

explanation.correct: Three specific actions scoped to specific resources: GetObject on A (read), PutObject on B (write), Publish on exact SNS ARN. Narrow on both action and resource axes — correct least privilege.
explanation.why: s3:* grants delete and policy modification beyond read/write. lambda:* manages Lambda infrastructure, not runtime. Option B is the only one narrow on both axes.

questions.question: A role trust policy contains: Principal: arn:aws:iam::999:role/CIRole, Action: sts:AssumeRole, Condition: StringEquals: sts:ExternalId: build-secret-42. CIRole tries to assume this role without providing ExternalId. What happens?

options.text: Success — conditions in trust policies are optional hints and not strictly enforced
Access Denied — ExternalId condition is required and enforced; AssumeRole call without matching ExternalId fails
Success — ExternalId is only checked for third-party service integrations
Access Denied — sts:ExternalId is only valid in identity-based policies, not trust policies

explanation.correct: Trust policy conditions are fully enforced. The AssumeRole call must include matching ExternalId or it fails with Access Denied. ExternalId prevents the confused deputy problem.
explanation.why: Trust policy conditions are as enforceable as any IAM condition. Without the matching value, assumption fails.

questions.question: A company's S3 bucket stores project data. Only principals tagged Project=Phoenix may access it. The rule must apply automatically as new roles are created. Most efficient approach?

options.text: Create a separate IAM policy for every role that needs access
Add a bucket policy condition: StringEquals: aws:PrincipalTag/Project: Phoenix — any principal carrying the correct tag automatically gets access
Create an IAM group called PhoenixGroup and reference it in the bucket policy
Use VPC endpoint policies to restrict access by project tag

explanation.correct: A bucket policy with aws:PrincipalTag condition automatically allows any principal tagged correctly — including new roles created in the future. Zero per-role management required.
explanation.why: Per-role policies require manual updates. IAM groups cannot be bucket policy principals. VPC endpoint policies control network path, not tag-based identity.

questions.question: Permission boundary on all Lambda execution roles does NOT include iam:CreateRole. A developer creates a new Lambda execution role and attaches AdministratorAccess. Can the Lambda create IAM roles?

options.text: Yes — AdministratorAccess overrides the permission boundary
No — effective permissions = intersection of AdministratorAccess and boundary; iam:CreateRole is absent from the boundary and therefore absent from effective permissions
Yes — permission boundaries only apply to IAM users, not roles
No — AdministratorAccess is entirely blocked by the boundary, so the Lambda has no permissions at all

explanation.correct: Effective permissions = intersection. AdministratorAccess includes iam:CreateRole. Boundary excludes it. Intersection removes it. Lambda cannot create IAM roles.
explanation.why: Permission boundaries apply to both users and roles. AdministratorAccess does not override boundaries. D is wrong — other permissions within the boundary still work.

questions.question: A Lambda execution role has: Effect: Allow, Action: iam:PassRole, Resource: *. Why is this a critical security finding?

options.text: iam:PassRole allows the Lambda to change its own execution role
iam:PassRole on Resource: * allows passing ANY role — including admin roles — to any AWS service that accepts roles, enabling privilege escalation to full account control
iam:PassRole is deprecated
iam:PassRole on Resource: * allows the Lambda to create new IAM users with admin access

explanation.correct: iam:PassRole required when passing a role to an AWS service (EC2, ECS, Glue). With Resource: *, the Lambda could pass an admin-level role to a new EC2 instance it launches — that instance runs with admin credentials.
explanation.why: iam:PassRole does not change your own role or create users. It enables passing roles to services — which is why Resource: * is so dangerous.

questions.question: Two teams need read access to S3 PII data. Neither should be able to delete under any circumstances, even if future policy changes accidentally grant delete. Minimum, most durable architecture?

options.text: Four policies — Allow-read per team, Deny-delete per team
Three policies — one shared Allow-read, two separate Deny-delete per team
Two policies — one shared Allow-read identity-based policy at group level, plus one bucket policy with explicit Deny on s3:DeleteObject for Principal: *
One bucket policy that both allows read for both teams and denies delete

explanation.correct: (1) One shared read policy at group level. (2) One bucket policy Deny DeleteObject for Principal: * — absolute and durable. The explicit Deny in a resource-based policy cannot be overridden by any future identity-based change.
explanation.why: D is architecturally possible but harder to maintain. Two policies (shared Allow + bucket Deny) is simpler and more durable.

questions.question: An account admin has AdministratorAccess. The account's OU has an SCP explicitly denying ec2:*. Can the admin launch EC2 instances?

options.text: Yes — AdministratorAccess overrides SCPs for account administrators
No — SCPs apply to all principals in the account including admins; SCP explicit Deny cannot be overridden by any identity-based Allow
Yes — SCPs only apply to non-admin IAM users
No — but only if the SCP was applied before AdministratorAccess was granted

explanation.correct: SCPs apply to every principal in member accounts including admins. An SCP Deny is a hard wall. No identity-based Allow including AdministratorAccess can override an SCP explicit Deny.
explanation.why: SCPs are evaluated before identity-based policies. AdministratorAccess has no override capability against SCPs.

questions.question: A developer assumes a role with AdministratorAccess and passes a session policy: Effect: Allow, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: *. What are the developer's effective permissions for this session?

options.text: AdministratorAccess — session policies cannot reduce the assumed role's permissions
Only s3:GetObject — session policies further limit (never expand) the assumed role's permissions; effective = intersection of role permissions and session policy
AdministratorAccess plus an extra explicit allow on s3:GetObject
No permissions — session policies completely replace role permissions

explanation.correct: Session policies passed at AssumeRole can only restrict, never expand permissions. Effective = intersection of role permissions AND session policy. Even with AdministratorAccess, session is limited to s3:GetObject only.
explanation.why: Session policies are a least-privilege tool for temporary scoped access. A common CI/CD and cross-account delegation pattern.

questions.question: A bucket policy: Effect: Deny, Principal: *, Action: s3:GetObject, Condition: StringNotEquals: aws:PrincipalOrgID: o-abc12345. Account X is a member of org o-abc12345. The instance role has s3:GetObject in its identity-based policy. What happens?

options.text: Allowed — Account X is in org o-abc12345; StringNotEquals evaluates to false; Deny condition not met; Deny does not fire
Denied — aws:PrincipalOrgID only works for cross-account requests
Denied — the instance is in Account X which is in org o-abc12345
Allowed regardless — instance role calls are exempt from bucket policy conditions

explanation.correct: The Deny fires when PrincipalOrgID is NOT o-abc12345. Account X IS in that org. StringNotEquals evaluates to false. Deny condition not satisfied. No Deny fires. Identity-based Allow grants access.
explanation.why: aws:PrincipalOrgID works for both same-account and cross-account. The condition: StringNotEquals with o-abc12345 means 'org is not o-abc12345.' If instance IS in that org, condition is false and Deny doesn't fire.

questions.question: A multi-tenant SaaS stores customer data under /tenant-A/, /tenant-B/ prefixes. Roles are tagged with TenantId. What IAM pattern enables one policy scoping each tenant to only their own prefix?

options.text: Condition: StringEquals: aws:RequestedRegion matching the tenant region
Resource: arn:aws:s3:::saas-bucket/${aws:PrincipalTag/TenantId}/* — policy variable dynamically constructs ARN from the calling role's TenantId tag
Create separate IAM policies per tenant with hardcoded prefix ARNs
A separate S3 bucket policy per tenant listing individual role ARNs

explanation.correct: IAM policy variables like ${aws:PrincipalTag/TenantId} dynamically construct the resource ARN from the caller's tag. A role tagged TenantId=tenant-A can only access /tenant-A/*. One policy, unlimited tenant scalability.
explanation.why: Per-tenant policies require manual management and don't scale. Region conditions have nothing to do with tenant isolation.

questions.question: A CI/CD pipeline role needs to deploy CloudFormation stacks that create EC2 instances, S3 buckets, and IAM roles. Security team worries about escalation via new roles. Most secure architecture?

options.text: Grant AdministratorAccess — it needs to create IAM roles anyway
Grant PowerUserAccess which excludes iam:*
Grant cloudformation:*, ec2:*, s3:*, iam:PassRole scoped to specific safe role ARNs — plus a permission boundary on the pipeline role excluding iam:CreateRole
Add aws:SourceIp condition limiting the pipeline role to the CI server IP

explanation.correct: Pipeline gets exactly what it needs. iam:PassRole scoped to safe ARNs (not *). Permission boundary prevents creating new IAM roles. Even if compromised, cannot escalate via new roles.
explanation.why: AdministratorAccess too broad. PowerUserAccess blocks iam:* but pipeline needs PassRole to deploy stacks with role attachments. Source IP is network-layer only.

questions.question: ABAC policy: Effect: Allow, Action: ec2:TerminateInstances, Condition: StringEquals: ec2:ResourceTag/Project: ${aws:PrincipalTag/Project}. Engineer tagged Project=Payments calls TerminateInstances on EC2 tagged Project=Inventory. Result?

options.text: Allowed — TerminateInstances does not support resource-level tag conditions
Denied — principal's Project tag (Payments) does not match the resource tag (Inventory); condition fails; implicit deny applies
Allowed — ABAC conditions only apply to create/write operations, not termination
Denied — ABAC requires the role and resource to share tag key AND value, plus an explicit Deny

explanation.correct: ABAC condition checks ec2:ResourceTag/Project against aws:PrincipalTag/Project. Engineer tag = Payments. Instance tag = Inventory. StringEquals = false. Allow condition fails. Implicit deny.
explanation.why: The condition failing means the Allow statement does not apply — not an explicit Deny. Result is implicit deny. EC2 TerminateInstances supports resource-level tag conditions.

questions.question: An unauthorized IAM user was created 3 weeks ago and exfiltrated data. Attacker used a compromised user to create the backdoor. Best preventive control going forward?

options.text: Enable CloudTrail in all regions and set up CloudWatch alarms for iam:CreateUser calls
Add a permission boundary to all IAM users preventing iam:CreateUser
Apply an SCP at the organization root denying iam:CreateUser for all principals except a dedicated IAM admin role — require MFA for that admin role
Use IAM Access Analyzer to detect new IAM users before exfiltration begins

explanation.correct: SCP at org root denying iam:CreateUser for all principals except admin role: automatic, account-wide, covers every new role and future account. Requiring MFA for the admin role adds friction.
explanation.why: CloudTrail alarms (A) detect but don't prevent. Permission boundaries (B) must be manually attached per user. Access Analyzer (D) finds external access issues, not insider user creation.

questions.question: Company uses S3 Object Lock in Governance mode. An engineer with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention calls DeleteObject on a locked object before retention date. Result?

options.text: Denied — Object Lock Governance mode cannot be bypassed by any IAM permission
Allowed — s3:BypassGovernanceRetention explicitly enables bypassing Governance locks when included in the request header
Allowed only if the IAM user also has AdministratorAccess
Denied — s3:BypassGovernanceRetention only works for Compliance mode

explanation.correct: Governance mode: can be bypassed by principals with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention plus the x-amz-bypass-governance-retention:true header. Compliance mode: cannot be bypassed by anyone including root.
explanation.why: Critical exam distinction. Compliance = absolutely immutable. Governance = protected against accidents, overridable with explicit permission.

questions.question: A policy must allow PutObject to S3 ONLY if objects are encrypted with a specific customer-managed KMS key (key ID abc-123). Which condition enforces this?

options.text: Condition: StringEquals: s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption: aws:kms
Condition: StringEquals: s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id: arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/abc-123
Condition: ArnEquals: kms:RequestAlias: alias/my-key
Condition: StringEquals: s3:kms-key-id: abc-123

explanation.correct: The condition key s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id matches the specific KMS key ARN used for SSE. StringEquals with the full key ARN ensures objects must be encrypted with exactly that key.
explanation.why: Option A only checks SSE-KMS is used, not which key. The full key ARN must be used. This enforces 'use our approved key or the write is denied.'

questions.question: Dev team and ops team both need read access to S3. Dev writes to /staging/; ops writes to /production/. Neither may write to the other's prefix. Design MINIMUM policies with MAXIMUM reuse.

options.text: Four policies: DevRead, OpsRead, DevWrite-staging, OpsWrite-production
Three policies: one shared Allow-read attached to both groups, plus DevWrite-staging and OpsWrite-production each scoped to their specific prefix
One bucket policy covering both teams' read and write
Two policies: one combined ReadWrite for dev (all prefixes), one ReadOnly for ops

explanation.correct: Three policies, maximum reuse: (1) One shared read policy for both groups. (2) DevWrite scoped to /staging/* only. (3) OpsWrite scoped to /production/* only. Narrow on both action and resource axes.
explanation.why: Four policies (A) has redundant DevRead and OpsRead. D grants cross-prefix write access which violates the requirement.

questions.question: CloudTrail shows: 10:00 alice assumes RoleA; 10:05 RoleA creates IAM user backdoor; 10:06 RoleA attaches AdministratorAccess to backdoor; 10:07 session expires; 10:08 backdoor exfiltrates. Which control prevents the 10:05 event?

options.text: MFA requirement on RoleA — blocks alice from assuming it without MFA
A permission boundary on RoleA not including iam:CreateUser — even if RoleA's identity-based policy allows it, the boundary excludes it from effective permissions
CloudTrail alerting on iam:CreateUser calls
A session policy passed during AssumeRole limiting RoleA to s3:GetObject

explanation.correct: Permission boundary on RoleA excluding iam:CreateUser prevents the 10:05 event. Regardless of identity-based policy, iam:CreateUser is not in the boundary and therefore not in effective permissions.
explanation.why: MFA wouldn't prevent an already-authenticated session. CloudTrail is reactive. Session policy scoped to s3:GetObject would break RoleA's other functionality — boundary is more surgical.

questions.question: Account A (central logging) S3 bucket policy lists Principal: [account-B-root, account-C-root, account-D-root]. New account E joins. What operational problem exists?

options.text: The bucket policy will break as new accounts join — only aws:PrincipalOrgID can handle dynamic org membership; explicit account root principals in bucket policies become stale
Every time a new account is added, the bucket policy must be manually updated — does not scale
Account root principals in bucket policies automatically replicate to new accounts
Accounts B, C, D would each need to replicate the bucket policy

explanation.correct: Listing individual account IDs doesn't scale. Every new account requires a manual bucket policy update. The scalable solution: use aws:PrincipalOrgID condition to cover all current and future org accounts automatically.
explanation.why: Cross-account principals in bucket policies are valid syntax. The operational problem is purely scaling.

questions.question: Data science team must re-authenticate with MFA every 30 minutes during S3 training sessions. Data must never leave the AWS network. Training on EC2. Which combination satisfies BOTH?

options.text: IAM role with aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 1800 (NumericLessThan) on S3 access, plus a VPC gateway endpoint for S3 ensuring traffic stays on the AWS network backbone
IAM role with aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true, plus S3 Transfer Acceleration
IAM role with aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 900, plus a bucket policy requiring aws:SecureTransport: true
IAM Identity Center with MFA enforcement at sign-in, plus VPC peering to the S3 region

explanation.correct: aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 1800 (NumericLessThan) = MFA required within last 30 minutes. VPC gateway endpoint for S3 = traffic flows through AWS backbone, never public internet.
explanation.why: MultiFactorAuthPresent (B) is session-wide, not per-30-minutes. aws:SecureTransport (C) enforces HTTPS but not private routing. VPC peering (D) connects VPCs; S3 uses endpoints, not peering.

questions.question: All S3 buckets across all Organization accounts must block public access including new accounts added in the future, with zero per-account configuration. Most complete, lowest-maintenance approach?

options.text: Lambda triggered by AccountCreation events to enable S3 Block Public Access per account
AWS Config organization conformance packs with s3-bucket-public-access-prohibited and auto-remediation
AWS Organizations S3 Block Public Access setting at the organization level — applies to all current and future accounts automatically with zero per-account action
SCP denying s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock to prevent anyone from disabling the setting

explanation.correct: AWS S3 Block Public Access organization-level setting applies to all member accounts automatically — new and existing. Single toggle in the management account. Zero per-account configuration.
explanation.why: Lambda (A) and Config (B) have operational overhead and gaps. SCP (D) prevents disabling but doesn't enable it on accounts where it isn't already on.

questions.question: CloudTrail shows AssumeRole to arn:aws:iam::999:role/AdminRole from an EC2 instance profile in account 888. Security team finds this suspicious. Which control prevents this assumption?

options.text: Globally disabling sts:AssumeRole from EC2 instance profiles
Restricting AdminRole trust policy to: Condition: StringEquals: aws:PrincipalAccount: 999 — same-account only
Modifying the AdminRole trust policy to remove account 888 as a trusted principal
Enabling real-time CloudTrail alerts on all sts:AssumeRole calls

explanation.correct: The AdminRole trust policy allows account 888. Removing account 888 from the Principal (or adding a blocking condition) prevents all future cross-account assumptions from account 888.
explanation.why: Blocking all EC2 instance profiles globally (A) breaks legitimate workloads. Restricting to same-account (B) breaks other legitimate cross-account uses. CloudTrail (D) is reactive.

questions.question: A company finds a role with: Effect: Allow, Action: sts:AssumeRole, Resource: *. What specific risk does this create?

options.text: The role can assume any role in the account — including admin roles — escalating to full account control
The role can assume any role in any AWS account worldwide with no restrictions
The role gains unlimited temporary permissions via STS automatically
Any external principal can assume this role

explanation.correct: sts:AssumeRole on Resource: * allows assuming ANY role in the account, including admin roles. This is a privilege escalation path to full account control. Fix: scope Resource to specific role ARNs this entity legitimately needs.
explanation.why: Cross-account assumption also requires the target account's trust policy. But in-account escalation to admin roles alone is critical.

questions.question: A bucket policy has: Effect: Deny, Principal: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:root, Action: s3:DeleteBucket. Does this prevent the account owner from deleting the bucket?

options.text: Yes — explicit Deny on account root in a bucket policy is effective; root is not exempt from resource-based policy explicit Denies
No — a bucket policy cannot Deny the account root; root has full access regardless
Yes — bucket policies with root Deny override all IAM controls including SCPs
No — only S3 Object Lock can prevent bucket deletion; IAM Deny statements cannot

explanation.correct: A bucket policy explicit Deny on the account root ARN IS effective. The root user is not exempt from explicit Denies in resource-based policies. This is one of the few mechanisms that can restrict what root can do in S3.
explanation.why: Root bypasses identity-based policy restrictions but NOT explicit Denies in resource-based policies.

questions.question: An application assumes a role with 1-hour credentials. 45 minutes in, it needs to run a 2-hour operation. Correct approach?

options.text: Stop and wait for credentials to expire before re-authenticating
Call sts:AssumeRole again before current credentials expire to get a new 1-hour token — well-designed AWS SDKs handle this automatically via refreshable credential providers
Call sts:ExtendSession to extend the current token's validity
Switch to IAM user access keys since temporary credentials are unsuitable for operations longer than 1 hour

explanation.correct: Applications should proactively refresh credentials before expiry. Calling sts:AssumeRole again gets a new token. AWS SDKs (boto3, Java SDK) handle this automatically via refreshable credential providers.
explanation.why: sts:ExtendSession does not exist. Stopping is unnecessary. IAM user access keys create credential management risk.

questions.question: An S3 bucket in Account A has a bucket policy that explicitly allows s3:GetObject for RoleX, which is also in Account A. RoleX has no identity-based policies that mention S3 at all. A junior engineer claims RoleX will get Access Denied because 'roles need their own S3 permission.' Is the junior engineer correct?

options.text: Yes — identity-based policy must also explicitly allow s3:GetObject; the bucket policy alone is never sufficient for IAM role access
No — for same-account access, a resource-based bucket policy explicitly granting RoleX is sufficient; no identity-based S3 policy on the role is required
Yes — bucket policies can only grant access to IAM users in the same account, not to IAM roles
No — but only because RoleX has no permission boundary; if a boundary existed the bucket policy alone would be insufficient

explanation.correct: The junior engineer is wrong. Same-account rule: one explicit Allow on either side (identity-based OR resource-based) is sufficient. The bucket policy's explicit Allow for RoleX grants access. RoleX does not also need an identity-based S3 policy. The 'both sides required' rule only applies to cross-account access.
explanation.why: A describes the cross-account requirement, not same-account. C is wrong — bucket policies can reference both users and roles. D is wrong — a permission boundary caps what policies can grant but doesn't create an additional authorization requirement for same-account resource-based policies.

questions.question: Developer role allows s3:PutObject on my-bucket/uploads/*. Bucket policy: Effect: Deny, Principal: *, Action: s3:PutObject, Condition: StringNotEquals: s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption: aws:kms. Developer calls PutObject without encryption header. What happens?

options.text: Success — identity-based policy allows PutObject and the bucket condition only applies to encrypted requests
Access Denied — bucket policy's Deny fires because unencrypted request lacks the aws:kms header; StringNotEquals is true; explicit Deny overrides identity-based Allow
Success — bucket policy conditions cannot evaluate request headers
Access Denied — S3 blocks all unencrypted PutObject requests by default

explanation.correct: Bucket policy: Deny PutObject when encryption header is NOT aws:kms. Unencrypted request has no SSE header set to aws:kms. StringNotEquals is true. Deny fires. Explicit Deny overrides identity-based Allow.
explanation.why: Standard 'enforce SSE-KMS on uploads' bucket policy pattern. S3 does not block unencrypted uploads by default — the bucket policy provides this enforcement.

questions.question: Compliance requirement: all API calls must be logged AND log integrity must be verifiable — no one should be able to delete or modify logs. Which architecture satisfies BOTH?

options.text: Enable CloudTrail in all regions; store logs in S3 with versioning enabled
Enable CloudTrail with log file validation; store logs in a separate logging account's S3 with Object Lock Compliance mode and a bucket policy denying DeleteObject from workload account principals
Enable CloudTrail with CloudWatch Logs integration; set retention to Never Expire
Enable AWS Config to detect CloudTrail log deletion and auto-remediate

explanation.correct: Multi-layer: (1) Log file validation = SHA-256 hash verification — tamper detection. (2) Separate logging account = workload admins have no access. (3) Object Lock Compliance = even logging account root cannot delete. Together these satisfy logging AND integrity.
explanation.why: Versioning (A) prevents deletion but allows modification of the current version. CloudWatch (C) doesn't provide integrity verification. Config (D) is reactive.

questions.question: On-call engineer needs emergency production database access. Requirements: no standing permissions, two-manager approval, all actions audited, access expires in 4 hours. Which approach satisfies ALL four?

options.text: Break-glass IAM user with database access stored in sealed envelope
AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with IAM roles, IAM Identity Center approval workflows, CloudTrail logging, and MaxSessionDuration set to 14400 seconds (4 hours) on the emergency role
Temporary IAM user with database permissions, manually deleted after 4 hours
Grant engineer's regular IAM user database access; revoke after 4 hours

explanation.correct: (1) No standing permissions = zero-standing role assumed only on approval. (2) Two-manager approval = Identity Center workflow. (3) All actions audited = CloudTrail + Session Manager logs. (4) 4-hour expiry = MaxSessionDuration = automatic expiry.
explanation.why: Break-glass users (A) have standing credentials. Temporary users (C) require manual cleanup and lack approval workflow. Regular user permissions (D) violate no-standing requirement.

questions.question: CI/CD pipeline role needs different permissions per environment (dev: full access, staging: read-write, prod: read-only). How to avoid three separate pipeline roles while maintaining environment-specific permissions?

options.text: One pipeline role with all permissions; use network ACLs to restrict which environment it reaches
One pipeline role with sts:AssumeRole; separate environment roles (DevRole, StagingRole, ProdRole) with appropriate permissions; pipeline assumes the relevant role per deployment
One pipeline role with broad permissions; add MFA conditions per environment tier
One pipeline role; use S3 bucket policies to restrict write access in staging and prod

explanation.correct: One pipeline identity, three environment roles. Each environment role has appropriately scoped permissions. ProdRole can require additional trust conditions. Separates deployment identity from environment permissions.
explanation.why: One role with all permissions (A) means compromised pipeline has prod write access. MFA conditions (C) complicate automation. Bucket policies (D) only cover S3.

questions.question: A Lambda execution role was used to call sts:GetCallerIdentity 500 times in one hour from an external IP. Function only runs once per day. What likely happened and what was the IAM failure?

options.text: Lambda has a code loop bug calling GetCallerIdentity 500 times per invocation

Lambda was storing access keys in environment variables; they were exfiltrated via SSRF or code injection; an attacker is using them externally — the IAM failure is using long-lived keys instead of relying solely on the execution role
The execution role's trust policy was misconfigured to allow external principals
Another Lambda in the same account is reusing this role's credentials

explanation.correct: External IP calls with Lambda credentials = stolen keys. Lambda should use execution roles only — not environment variable access keys. Keys in env vars can be exfiltrated. Execution role credentials are scoped to AWS IPs and cannot be used externally.
explanation.why: Execution role credentials are delivered via metadata service and scoped to AWS IPs. External calls mean long-lived keys were exfiltrated from environment variables or code.

questions.question: A company wants developers to create IAM roles for applications ONLY if those roles have a specific permission boundary attached. Developers must not create roles without the boundary. Which policy combination enforces this?

options.text: Condition: StringEquals: iam:PermissionsBoundary: arn:...:policy/DevBoundary on the Allow statement only
Condition: Null: iam:PermissionsBoundary: true on a Deny statement only
Both: Allow iam:CreateRole with Condition: StringEquals: iam:PermissionsBoundary: arn:...:policy/DevBoundary, AND Deny iam:CreateRole with Condition: Null: iam:PermissionsBoundary: true
A permission boundary on the developer's own role that excludes iam:CreateRole entirely

explanation.correct: Complete enforcement needs two statements: (1) Allow iam:CreateRole only when the correct boundary is specified. (2) Deny iam:CreateRole when NO boundary is specified (Null: true = key is absent). This is the canonical delegated admin IAM pattern.
explanation.why: A alone allows with correct boundary but doesn't prevent creating with a different boundary. B alone denies absent boundary but doesn't enforce which boundary. C together is comprehensive.

questions.question: Audit team needs read access to S3 reports ONLY from corporate network IP 203.0.113.0/24. Remote access must be blocked even for authorized users. Strongest absolute enforcement?

options.text: Condition: IpAddress: aws:SourceIp: 203.0.113.0/24 in an Allow statement on the identity-based policy
Condition: NotIpAddress: aws:SourceIp: 203.0.113.0/24 in a Deny statement on the bucket policy — denies access when source IP is NOT in the corporate range
Condition: IpAddress: aws:VpcSourceIp: 203.0.113.0/24 in a VPC endpoint policy
Both A and B are valid; B on the bucket policy provides stronger absolute enforcement via resource-level explicit Deny that cannot be overridden by identity-based policy changes

explanation.correct: Both work. A (identity-based Allow with IpAddress) requires source IP to match. B (bucket policy Deny with NotIpAddress) is stronger: explicit Deny at resource level — even future identity-based policy changes cannot override it.
explanation.why: aws:SourceIp applies to public IPs. aws:VpcSourceIp applies to VPC endpoint calls — different use case. The explicit Deny on the bucket (B) is the stronger absolute enforcement mechanism.

questions.question: 50 AWS accounts need to ensure no IAM user has access keys older than 90 days. Must be automated across all accounts. Most automated approach?

options.text: Weekly Lambda checking all IAM users across accounts and emailing administrators about old keys

Organization-level AWS Config conformance pack with iam-user-unused-credentials-check and Systems Manager Automation for auto-remediation — deactivates keys older than 90 days across all accounts automatically
SCP that denies all API calls when the caller's access key age exceeds 90 days using a NumericGreaterThan condition on aws:CredentialAge
Condition: NumericGreaterThan: aws:CredentialAge: 90 Deny added to all identity-based policies

explanation.correct: AWS Config organization conformance packs deploy compliance rules across all accounts simultaneously. Combined with SSM Automation for auto-remediation, old keys are automatically deactivated without human intervention.
explanation.why: Lambda/Lambda (A) is reactive and has a 24-hour gap. SCPs (C) cannot evaluate credential age — aws:CredentialAge is not a real IAM condition key and SCPs do not have access to session metadata about when credentials were created. aws:CredentialAge (D) is not a real condition key — Config with auto-remediation is the only automated cross-account solution.

questions.question: Access Denied despite: SCP = no restriction, identity-based = Allow s3:GetObject, permission boundary = allows GetObject, bucket policy = no statement, session policy = Effect: Allow, Action: s3:GetObject. The application also calls s3:ListBucket in the same code path. Most likely actual cause?

options.text: The session policy should be Effect: Deny to work correctly
The session policy explicitly lists only s3:GetObject; s3:ListBucket calls in the application are denied by implicit deny in the session policy — ListBucket is not listed
Bucket policies with no statements default to Deny for all calls
Session policies and permission boundaries cannot coexist

explanation.correct: The session policy only allows s3:GetObject. When the application also calls s3:ListBucket, that action is NOT in the session policy. Session policies apply implicit deny to everything not listed.
explanation.why: The session policy itself is not wrong — the problem is the application needs more actions than the session policy allows.

questions.question: A company needs to share a KMS key across ALL current and future accounts in their Organization without updating the key policy when new accounts join. Which key policy condition achieves this?

options.text: Condition: StringEquals: aws:PrincipalAccount: * — wildcard for all accounts
Condition: StringEquals: aws:PrincipalOrgID: o-xxxxxxxxxx — allows any principal whose account belongs to the organization
Condition: StringEquals: kms:CallerAccount: org-all — using the org alias
Condition: ArnLike: aws:PrincipalArn: arn:aws:iam::*:root — allows all account root users

explanation.correct: aws:PrincipalOrgID with the organization ID covers all current and future member accounts automatically. New accounts joining the org automatically get KMS access without any key policy update.
explanation.why: aws:PrincipalAccount: * is not valid syntax. kms:CallerAccount doesn't support org aliases. ArnLike with :root only allows root users, not IAM roles or users.

questions.question: During a red team exercise, attacker has an EC2 instance profile with s3:GetObject on all buckets. Which additional permission represents the HIGHEST privilege escalation risk?

options.text: s3:ListAllMyBuckets — allows the attacker to enumerate all bucket names in the account and identify high-value targets for further exploitation

iam:PassRole with Resource: * — allows passing any IAM role including admin roles to any AWS service that accepts them, enabling the attacker to launch a new EC2 instance with an admin role and gain full account control
ec2:DescribeInstances — allows the attacker to map the entire EC2 fleet, identify instance types, tags, and network configuration for lateral movement planning
cloudwatch:PutMetricData — allows the attacker to publish fake metrics that could manipulate Auto Scaling policies or trigger misleading CloudWatch alarms

explanation.correct: iam:PassRole on Resource: * allows passing any IAM role — including admin roles — to any AWS service that accepts them. The attacker can launch a new EC2 instance with an admin role attached, then access that instance to use its admin credentials. Full account compromise.
explanation.why: s3:ListAllMyBuckets enables reconnaissance but not escalation. ec2:DescribeInstances and cloudwatch:PutMetricData have no escalation path. iam:PassRole: * is consistently the highest-risk IAM permission.

questions.question: A new engineer's IdP account exists but they are not yet provisioned in IAM Identity Center and have no permission set assignments. They try to log in to the AWS console. What happens?

options.text: Login succeeds — Identity Center syncs with IdP in real time
Login fails — engineer must be provisioned in Identity Center (via SCIM or manual) AND have permission sets assigned to at least one account before accessing the console
Login succeeds but with read-only access until permissions are explicitly granted
Login fails at the IdP — AWS controls when IdP accounts are created

explanation.correct: Identity Center requires two things: (1) User provisioned in Identity Center via SCIM or manual creation. (2) Permission set assigned to the user for a specific account. Without both, no access even if IdP account exists.
explanation.why: Real-time sync is not guaranteed without SCIM. Identity Center does not grant default read-only. AWS does not control IdP account creation.

questions.question: A bucket policy uses aws:SourceVpc to restrict S3 access. An EC2 instance in the VPC calls GetObject and gets Access Denied despite the bucket policy allowing the VPC. The instance role has s3:GetObject. Most common cause?

options.text: The EC2 instance role's s3:GetObject policy must include the VPC ID
aws:SourceVpc only evaluates when requests come through a VPC endpoint for S3; if EC2 routes S3 traffic through an internet gateway, the condition key is not set and the bucket policy Deny fires
aws:SourceVpc requires a matching SCP to be effective
EC2 instance and bucket must be in the same Availability Zone for aws:SourceVpc to evaluate

explanation.correct: aws:SourceVpc and aws:SourceVpce conditions only evaluate when requests pass through a VPC endpoint. If S3 traffic routes through an internet gateway (even in the same VPC), no VPC endpoint is in the path, the condition key is absent, and the bucket policy Deny fires. Fix: create an S3 VPC gateway endpoint.
explanation.why: Critical production gotcha. The identity-based policy may have s3:GetObject, but the bucket policy Deny for non-endpoint requests fires when traffic bypasses the endpoint.

questions.question: An IAM policy attached to an EC2 instance role states: Effect: Deny, Action: *, Resource: *, Condition: Bool: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: false. What is the practical result?

options.text: All API calls are denied unless MFA was used to authenticate the session
All API calls from this role are always denied — IAM roles and instance profiles never set aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent to true; it is always false or absent for role credentials
API calls from EC2 are always denied because instance profiles cannot satisfy any MFA conditions
This policy has no effect — Deny with Action: * is not valid IAM syntax

explanation.correct: IAM roles (EC2 instance profiles, Lambda execution roles) do NOT set aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent to true. Only human users who explicitly authenticate with MFA set it. For roles, MultiFactorAuthPresent is always false or absent. This Deny fires for every call.
explanation.why: Critical gotcha. This policy is intended for human IAM users but when attached to a role it blocks everything. Use MFA conditions ONLY on IAM user policies, not role policies.

questions.question: A company's S3 bucket was accidentally public for 6 hours. S3 Block Public Access was disabled. Security team needs to audit unauthenticated public reads. Which service provides the MOST complete answer?

options.text: AWS Config — shows historical bucket policy configuration changes
S3 Server Access Logs (if enabled) — captures every HTTP request including anonymous public reads with requester IP, object key, and timestamp
VPC Flow Logs — captures all network traffic to S3 endpoints
CloudTrail S3 data events — captures all authenticated API calls on the bucket

explanation.correct: Anonymous public S3 reads do NOT appear in CloudTrail because there is no authenticating identity. Only S3 Server Access Logs capture anonymous HTTP requests — including every unauthenticated read with requester IP, object key, and timestamp.
explanation.why: CloudTrail only captures authenticated API calls. Config shows configuration history, not access events. VPC Flow Logs capture network metadata, not application-level S3 request details.

questions.question: A fintech Lambda execution role has ONLY: Effect: Allow, Action: dynamodb:PutItem, Resource: specific-table-ARN. Can a compromised Lambda read, modify, or delete existing records? A board member says no additional Deny statements are needed. Correct?

options.text: No — dynamodb:PutItem implicitly grants read access for conditional writes
Yes — the policy grants exactly PutItem; AWS implicit deny applies to all other DynamoDB actions including GetItem, UpdateItem, DeleteItem, Query, and Scan
No — DynamoDB requires at least GetItem permission to perform PutItem
Yes — but only if a DynamoDB resource policy also explicitly denies read/update/delete

explanation.correct: The board member is correct. Policy grants exactly PutItem on the specific table. AWS is deny-by-default: ALL other DynamoDB actions (GetItem, UpdateItem, DeleteItem, Query, Scan) are implicitly denied. No additional Deny statements needed.
explanation.why: DynamoDB does not require GetItem to perform PutItem. PutItem does not grant implicit read access. Implicit deny on all unlisted actions is exactly how least privilege works.

questions.question: A Lambda execution role has dynamodb:PutItem scoped to the exact table ARN. A reviewer says 'add dynamodb:DescribeTable so the function can check the table exists at startup.' Following strict least privilege, correct response?

options.text: Add dynamodb:DescribeTable on Resource: * since DescribeTable is read-only and harmless
Add dynamodb:DescribeTable scoped to the same specific table ARN only if the function genuinely calls DescribeTable at runtime — verify in code first
Reject the suggestion entirely — Lambda functions should never call DescribeTable
Add the entire dynamodb:Describe* wildcard for all future describe operations

explanation.correct: Least privilege: add permissions only for actions the function ACTUALLY calls. Verify in code whether DescribeTable is genuinely needed. If yes, add it scoped to the exact table ARN. Never add permissions speculatively.
explanation.why: Resource: * (A) is unnecessarily broad. Rejecting any operational need (C) is inflexible. Wildcard Describe* (D) grants more than needed.

questions.question: Organization SCPs: root OU has Allow: *, Resource: *. A specific OU has Deny: ec2:*, Resource: *. An account admin in that OU has AdministratorAccess. Which services can they use?

options.text: All services including EC2 — root OU Allow: * overrides the OU-level Deny
All services EXCEPT EC2 — the OU-level SCP Deny on ec2:* cannot be overridden by any identity-based Allow including AdministratorAccess
No services — conflicting SCPs at different OU levels result in total denial
EC2 only — the specific OU SCP takes precedence over the root OU SCP

explanation.correct: SCP evaluation: the account inherits SCPs from all parent OUs. Root OU allows everything. The specific OU denies ec2:*. Explicit Deny in any SCP wins — the admin cannot use EC2. All other services are unaffected.
explanation.why: SCP Deny at any level in the hierarchy wins over Allow at any other level.

questions.question: A CISO wants to ensure that if an AWS member account is fully compromised — attacker gains admin access — they cannot disable GuardDuty, CloudTrail, or Security Hub. Architectural answer?

options.text: Enable MFA Delete on the S3 bucket storing CloudTrail logs
Apply permission boundaries on all admin roles excluding security service destruction actions

Apply an SCP from the management account denying guardduty:DeleteDetector, cloudtrail:DeleteTrail, securityhub:DeleteHub for all member account principals — compromised account admin cannot override a management account SCP
Enable CloudTrail organization trail so deletion in one region is still logged in others

explanation.correct: An SCP from the management account applies to ALL principals in member accounts — including those with admin access — and cannot be modified from within the member account. Even a fully compromised admin cannot disable these controls.
explanation.why: MFA Delete only protects S3 objects. Permission boundaries must be individually applied — an admin could remove them. Multi-region CloudTrail doesn't prevent deletion. SCP from management account is the immutable guardrail.

questions.question: A developer writes: Effect: Allow, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: *, Condition: StringEquals: s3:prefix: [quarterly/, annual/]. They expect this to limit GetObject to only those prefixes. Does it work?

options.text: Yes — the s3:prefix condition restricts GetObject to only those two prefixes
No — s3:prefix is a condition key for s3:ListBucket only; it has NO effect on s3:GetObject. The policy actually allows GetObject on ALL objects in all buckets because the condition does not apply.
Yes — s3:prefix works for both ListBucket and GetObject
No — the Condition element cannot be combined with s3:GetObject

explanation.correct: s3:prefix condition key applies ONLY to s3:ListBucket — it restricts which objects are listed. It has NO effect on s3:GetObject. The policy allows GetObject on ALL objects in ALL buckets (Resource: *) because the condition is silently ignored. Correct restriction for GetObject is via the Resource ARN.
explanation.why: s3:prefix is documented as a condition for ListBucket. Using it on GetObject is a silent no-op — the condition doesn't evaluate and Resource: * is the effective scope.

questions.question: A CloudFormation StackSet execution role needs iam:CreateRole, iam:AttachRolePolicy, and iam:PassRole. Security team wants to prevent creation of admin-level roles during deployments. Most surgical control?

options.text: Add iam:CreateRole to a Deny statement in the StackSet execution role's policy — prevents all role creation
Add a permission boundary to the StackSet execution role excluding iam:CreateRole entirely
Scope iam:PassRole to specific safe role ARNs; add Condition on iam:CreateRole requiring iam:PermissionsBoundary: arn:...:policy/SafeBoundary — ensures all created roles have the safety boundary
SCP denying iam:CreateRole in all member accounts where StackSets deploy

explanation.correct: StackSet role NEEDS iam:CreateRole for its job. Surgical fix: allow CreateRole but require iam:PermissionsBoundary to be set to a specific safe boundary ARN. Scope iam:PassRole to safe role ARNs. Every role created has the boundary — preventing admin-level effective permissions.
explanation.why: Denying CreateRole entirely (A, B) breaks the StackSet's purpose. SCP (D) would block all accounts from creating roles — too broad.

questions.question: A security engineer needs to audit which IAM principals have access to a specific S3 bucket, including bucket policy grants, cross-account role assumptions, and identity-based policies. Most comprehensive approach?

options.text: Manually read the bucket policy and list all roles with s3:GetObject across all accounts
Use IAM Access Analyzer to analyze the bucket — it maps all access paths including cross-account, org-level grants, and public access using automated formal reasoning
Query CloudTrail for all s3:GetObject calls in the last 90 days
Use AWS Config to check the bucket's current resource-based policy

explanation.correct: IAM Access Analyzer uses automated formal reasoning to find ALL principals that have access — through bucket policies, identity-based policies, cross-account role assumptions, and org-level conditions. Complete access map that manual review cannot match.
explanation.why: Manual review (A) misses identity-based paths and cross-account scenarios. CloudTrail (C) shows historical access but misses principals who haven't accessed yet. Config (D) shows policy but doesn't analyze the full access graph.

questions.question: A company has a break-glass IAM role used only in emergencies. They want IMMEDIATE notification (within seconds) if this role is ever assumed. Most responsive detection?

options.text: Daily CloudTrail report filtered for AssumeRole events on this role
AWS Config rule detecting when the role is used — 15-minute polling delay
Amazon EventBridge rule matching CloudTrail AssumeRole events for the specific role ARN, triggering SNS to the security team — notification within seconds of assumption
IAM Access Analyzer continuous monitoring alerting when the role is assumed

explanation.correct: EventBridge + CloudTrail provides near-real-time detection. CloudTrail events flow to EventBridge. An EventBridge rule filters for eventName: AssumeRole AND requestParameters.roleArn = break-glass-ARN. Triggers SNS within seconds.
explanation.why: Daily reports = 24-hour gap. Config = up to 15-minute delay. Access Analyzer analyzes policies, not runtime events. EventBridge + CloudTrail is the standard real-time IAM event detection pattern.

questions.question: An engineer says: 'A policy with Effect: Allow, Action: *, Resource: * is always a security violation.' A colleague cites AdministratorAccess. Who is correct?

options.text: The engineer — Action: *, Resource: * is always a security violation
