The colleague — AdministratorAccess (Effect: Allow, Action: *, Resource: *) is a legitimate AWS managed policy appropriate for designated account administrators, when combined with MFA, CloudTrail, SCPs, and permission boundaries
The colleague — Action: *, Resource: * with Effect: Allow is acceptable in any role that needs to manage more than 10 AWS services simultaneously
Both are partially correct — it is only appropriate for the root user

explanation.correct: AdministratorAccess is a legitimate AWS managed policy with Effect: Allow, Action: *, Resource: *. Appropriate for designated admin identities with proper safeguards: MFA, CloudTrail, SCPs, and permission boundaries where needed.
explanation.why: Blanket statements ignoring context are wrong. AdministratorAccess is a core AWS primitive. The controls around it provide the necessary guardrails.

questions.question: A company wants to prevent all new S3 buckets from being created without server-side encryption, with zero per-bucket configuration. Simplest approach?

options.text: AWS Config rule s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled with auto-remediation
SCP denying s3:CreateBucket when SSE configuration is absent from the request
Enable S3 default encryption at the account level — all new buckets automatically inherit the default encryption setting
CloudFormation template deployed to every new bucket requiring SSE headers

explanation.correct: Enabling S3 default encryption at the account level means every new bucket automatically inherits the encryption setting. No SCP, no Config rule, no per-bucket action needed.
explanation.why: Config (A) is reactive. SCPs (B) for s3:CreateBucket with SSE conditions are complex and fragile. CloudFormation templates (D) require deployment to every new bucket.

questions.question: A developer has PowerUserAccess (Effect: Allow, NotAction: [iam:*, organizations:*], Resource: *) plus a custom policy: Effect: Allow, Action: [iam:GetUser, iam:ListUsers], Resource: *. Which actions can they call?

options.text: All AWS actions including full IAM management — the custom policy overrides PowerUserAccess exclusions
All non-IAM AWS actions plus iam:GetUser and iam:ListUsers — multiple Allows are evaluated as a union; custom policy adds specific IAM read actions
Only iam:GetUser and iam:ListUsers — PowerUserAccess restricts all other services
All non-IAM AWS actions only — the custom IAM read policy is ignored because PowerUserAccess uses NotAction to exclude iam:*

explanation.correct: Multiple policies attached to the same principal: all Allows are unioned. PowerUserAccess allows everything except iam:* and organizations:*. Custom policy adds iam:GetUser and iam:ListUsers. Together: all non-IAM permissions plus those two IAM read actions.
explanation.why: Policies are evaluated together — multiple Allows union. The custom policy adds to PowerUserAccess. The developer gets both sets combined.

questions.question: 100 EC2 Spot Instances run 5 job types, each accessing different S3 prefixes and DynamoDB tables. CTO proposes one shared IAM role for all instances. Primary security argument against this?

options.text: IAM does not support multiple EC2 instances sharing a single role
A single role means every job type has access to every other job type's data — a compromised Job A instance can read and write Job B, C, D, E data; separate per-job-type roles contain blast radius
A single role cannot hold enough policies to cover 5 different job types' permissions
Shared instance roles create incorrect cost allocation in AWS Cost Explorer

explanation.correct: Least privilege for batch workloads: each job type should have a role scoped to exactly its S3 prefixes and DynamoDB tables. Compromised Job A instance with shared role can access all other jobs' data. Separate roles contain blast radius to exactly one job type.
explanation.why: Multiple instances can share roles — that is how instance profiles work. Policy limits are generous enough. Cost allocation uses tags. The security argument is blast radius containment.

questions.question: Complex IAM evaluation: SCP (no relevant statement), identity-based (explicit Allow), permission boundary (explicit Allow), resource-based (no statement, same-account), session policy (explicit Allow). What is the result?

options.text: Allowed — all three Allows present with no Deny anywhere
Denied — the resource-based policy has no Allow, which acts as implicit Deny for resource-based evaluation
Allowed — only the identity-based Allow is needed; boundary and session Allows are redundant
Denied — all five policy types must have explicit Allows for access to be granted

explanation.correct: Step 1: any explicit Deny? No. Step 2: any explicit Allow? Yes — identity-based, boundary, and session policy all allow it. For same-account, this is sufficient. Resource-based policy absence is not a Deny for same-account. Allow is granted.
explanation.why: Not all policy types must have explicit Allows. Absence of resource-based policy statement is not a Deny for same-account. The 'both required' rule only applies to cross-account.

questions.question: A platform team wants every IAM role created via CloudFormation StackSets to automatically be unable to call iam:* actions, regardless of what the template specifies. Automated enforcement mechanism?

options.text: Add iam:* to a Deny statement in every CloudFormation template — manual and forgettable

Create a permission boundary policy excluding iam:*; configure the CloudFormation execution role to always attach this boundary when creating roles via iam:PermissionsBoundary condition on iam:CreateRole
Apply an SCP denying iam:* in all accounts where StackSets deploy
Train platform engineers not to include iam:* in StackSet templates

explanation.correct: Engineering solution: the StackSet execution role's iam:CreateRole permission requires iam:PermissionsBoundary to be set to the NoIAMBoundary ARN. The boundary policy excludes iam:*. Every role created via StackSets automatically has this boundary — regardless of what the template specifies.
explanation.why: Per-template Deny (A) is manual and can be omitted. SCP (C) would block the CF execution role itself. Training (D) is not a technical control.

questions.question: Several member accounts have the management account's root user ARN as a trusted principal in cross-account roles. What specific security risk does this create beyond normal cross-account access?

options.text: The management account root has more permissions than needed for cross-account operations
The management account root is exempt from SCPs — if compromised, it can assume roles in all member accounts AND actions taken via those roles in member accounts are not SCP-constrained
Cross-account trust policies listing root ARNs are invalid and will silently fail
The management account root would conflict with member account IAM Identity Center users

explanation.correct: SCPs do not apply to the management account's root user. If an attacker compromises it, they can assume cross-account roles in all member accounts AND the resulting session bypasses SCP constraints that would normally apply to member account principals.
explanation.why: Best practice: never list management account root in member account trust policies. Use specific IAM roles in the management account instead.

questions.question: A company wants only their VPC to access their S3 bucket — no access via public internet, even from authorized IAM users working remotely. Which combination achieves this?

options.text: Bucket policy with Condition: IpAddress: aws:SourceIp: VPC-CIDR-range
S3 VPC gateway endpoint plus a bucket policy with Condition: StringNotEquals: aws:SourceVpce: vpce-xxxxx in a Deny statement — denies all requests NOT via the specific VPC endpoint
VPC security group blocking all outbound S3 traffic except from specific instances
Enabling S3 Block Public Access — this restricts access to VPC-only routing

explanation.correct: Correct pattern: (1) S3 VPC gateway endpoint routes S3 traffic through AWS backbone. (2) Bucket policy Deny with StringNotEquals aws:SourceVpce denies all requests NOT via the VPC endpoint. Authorized remote users go via internet (no endpoint) and fail the condition.
explanation.why: aws:SourceIp matches public IPs — remote workers and attackers share public IPs making this unreliable. Security groups control instance egress. S3 Block Public Access blocks public bucket policies, not VPC-only routing.

questions.question: Account B's auditor role needs to call iam:GenerateCredentialReport and iam:GetCredentialReport in Account A. What must be configured?

options.text: An IAM role in Account A with trust policy allowing Account B's auditor role, with iam:GenerateCredentialReport and iam:GetCredentialReport permissions
A resource-based policy on Account A's IAM credential report resource allowing Account B's auditor role
An SCP in Account A's organization allowing Account B to call IAM actions cross-account
Account B's auditor role directly, with IAM permissions scoped to Account A's account ID

explanation.correct: IAM does not support resource-based policies on its own resources. For cross-account IAM access: create a role in Account A with trust policy allowing Account B's auditor to assume it. Attach IAM read permissions to this cross-account role. Account B's auditor assumes the role via STS.
explanation.why: IAM has no resource-based policies. SCPs set guardrails but don't grant permissions. Account B's role cannot directly call IAM APIs in Account A without assuming a role there first.

questions.question: Developer role has Policy 1: Allow s3:GetObject on bucket-A/*. Policy 2: Effect: Deny, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::bucket-A/sensitive/*. They call GetObject on bucket-A/sensitive/report.pdf. Result?

options.text: Allowed — Policy 1 grants access; Policy 2's Deny applies at the prefix level not individual objects
Denied — Policy 2's explicit Deny on bucket-A/sensitive/* matches the request; explicit Deny from any attached policy overrides Allow from any other attached policy
Allowed — when two identity-based policies conflict, the Allow takes precedence
Denied — conflicting policies always produce implicit Deny, not explicit

explanation.correct: bucket-A/sensitive/report.pdf matches bucket-A/sensitive/* (wildcard covers all objects under that prefix). Policy 2's explicit Deny fires. Explicit Deny in any attached policy overrides Allow in any other attached policy.
explanation.why: The three-step rule applies across all attached policies. Explicit Deny in Policy 2 wins over Allow in Policy 1. Option D is wrong — it IS an explicit Deny from Policy 2.

questions.question: Five policy types all apply: SCP = explicit Deny (condition met), identity-based = explicit Allow, permission boundary = explicit Allow, bucket policy = explicit Allow, session policy = explicit Allow. Four Allows vs one Deny. Result?

options.text: Allowed — four Allows outweigh one Deny by majority
Denied — the SCP explicit Deny triggers Step 1 of the evaluation rule; all four Allows are irrelevant once any explicit Deny is found
Allowed — SCPs only restrict when no other policy type grants an Allow
Denied — conflicting policies from different types always produce denial

explanation.correct: Step 1: any explicit Deny anywhere? Yes — SCP explicit Deny. Evaluation stops. Denied. It doesn't matter that four other policies allow the action. IAM evaluation is not a voting system.
explanation.why: One explicit Deny beats 100 Allows. This is the most fundamental IAM invariant and is tested in exactly this format on SAA-C03.

questions.question: Fintech CISO requirements: (1) no long-lived access keys anywhere, (2) all API calls audited, (3) production deletion requires MFA issued within 5 minutes, (4) developers cannot escalate to admin. Which COMBINATION addresses ALL four?

options.text: IAM users with access keys + CloudTrail + MFA at sign-in only + AdministratorAccess for developers
IAM roles via instance profiles + CloudTrail data events + aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 300 (NumericLessThan) on deletion policies + permission boundaries on developer roles
STS temporary credentials + AWS Config + aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true on deletion policies + SCPs
IAM Identity Center + GuardDuty + MFA at sign-in + SCP denying admin access

explanation.correct: (1) IAM roles via instance profiles = no long-lived access keys. (2) CloudTrail data events = all API calls audited including data-plane. (3) aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 300 NumericLessThan = MFA within last 5 minutes for deletion. (4) Permission boundaries on developer roles = cap maximum permissions, no admin escalation.
explanation.why: A uses long-lived access keys (violates 1) and gives developers admin (violates 4). MultiFactorAuthPresent (C) doesn't enforce 5-minute recency (violates 3). GuardDuty (D) detects threats but doesn't enforce MFA recency.

questions.question: A bucket policy in Account A grants s3:GetObject to a role in Account B. The Account B role has NO identity-based policy allowing s3:GetObject on Account A's bucket. A developer says 'bucket policies override identity-based policies so this works.' Correct?

options.text: Yes — resource-based bucket policy alone is always sufficient for both same-account and cross-account access

No — cross-account requires explicit Allow on both sides; the bucket policy (destination) is present but the role's identity-based policy (source) has no Allow; implicit deny at the source blocks the call
Yes — bucket policy in Account A is sufficient for cross-account access since it explicitly names the Account B role
No — bucket policies cannot grant cross-account access; only STS role assumption works

explanation.correct: Cross-account requires explicit Allow on BOTH sides. Bucket policy in Account A = destination-side Allow present. Role in Account B has no identity-based Allow = source side missing. Implicit deny applies at the source account. The call fails.
explanation.why: A is correct for same-account (bucket policy alone suffices) but wrong for cross-account. D is wrong — bucket policies CAN enable cross-account when both sides authorize. B correctly describes the cross-account both-sides requirement.
